clue.text: Jewel thief raised feeling of dread, did you say? (7)

indicators.note: Asking whether you said it puts the wordplay in your mouth: what counts is the noise two words make run together, not how either is spelt.

blocks.note: to jack something up is to raise it
awe is the mixture of wonder and dread that something overwhelming produces
said as one, the two words fall across a different join and come out as seven letters

annotation.surface: Somebody checking they heard right about a jewel thief who left everyone frightened.
annotation.walkthrough: The bird is famous for carrying off anything bright and shiny, which is what lets a species answer to a charge of theft. Nothing is spelt out here; the whole clue is a noise.
annotation.definitionFit: Jewel thief → JACKDAW: the bird has a reputation for stealing glittering objects for its nest, so the human crime is pinned on it.

clue.text: Marked by convulsions, that must be cured (5)

definitions.note: The first definition is a plain adjective and the second describes a foodstuff, so the answer changes part of speech between the two halves of the clue.

blocks.note: the adjective for movement that arrives in sudden uncontrolled tugs
strips of meat salted and dried until they will keep without a fridge

annotation.surface: A twitchy patient whose condition needs treating.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cured' is the hinge: it means treated by a doctor in the surface and salted and dried in the answer, which is what turns strips of beef into a snack.
annotation.definitionFit: Jerky movement is a series of jerks, and jerky the food is meat that has to be cured and dried before it will keep.

clue.text: True self critical of drink (7)

blocks.note: chi is the life force of Chinese philosophy, the energy held to be a person's innermost self
anti means set against something, which is what being critical of it comes to

annotation.surface: Someone being true to themselves and disapproving of the drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: Chi is worth banking: crosswords use those three letters for life force, spirit or inner energy whenever a clue turns mystical. The definition is the last word alone.
annotation.definitionFit: drink → CHIANTI: the dry red wine of Tuscany, so the definition names the class and the answer supplies one example of it.

clue.text: Shatter bolt (4)

blocks.note: to smash a thing to pieces, the verb used of hopes that come to nothing
the verb rather than the door fitting: to run off suddenly

annotation.surface: A bolt being smashed apart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bolt' looks like the noun on a door, which is what makes the two words read as one instruction; the answer needs it as a verb, to run for it.
annotation.definitionFit: To dash something is to smash it — dashed hopes, dashed to pieces — and to dash is also to bolt, to leave at speed.

clue.text: How would you like to go – for a drink? (5,4,6)

definitions.text: How would you like to go – for a drink?

blocks.clueFragment: How would you like to go
blocks.note: The surface offers this as a question about travel arrangements; the setter means it as a question about how you would choose to die.
The second reading is the one heard across a bar, where the same question is only asking which bottle to reach for.

annotation.surface: One friend asking another how they fancy getting to the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash is where the clue changes register: everything before it belongs to an execution and everything after it to a night out, and the phrase serves both.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase is a barman's dated way of asking what to pour, and it takes 'poison' literally enough to double as a question about dying.

clue.text: Taken to the cleaners, as are duvets and mattresses (7)

definitions.note: The second definition works by example rather than by synonym: it names two things the word is true of instead of offering another word for it.

blocks.note: the idiom for being comprehensively beaten, cheated or fleeced
both are packed full of filling, which is the literal sense of the word

annotation.surface: Bedding on its way to the laundry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taken to the cleaners' is idiom rather than laundry — it means comprehensively beaten or fleeced — and the duvets are there to make the phrase sound like a delivery note.
annotation.definitionFit: Taken to the cleaners means thoroughly beaten or robbed; duvets and mattresses are stuffed in the literal sense, packed full of filling.

clue.text: If it’s the last thing you do, visit the home of pizza: need pasta in Leeds? No time for it, unfortunately (3,6,3,3)

definitions.text: If it’s the last thing you do, visit the home of pizza

indicators.note: Having no time for something is refusing to give it house room, and time is T, so that letter is refused a place among the rest.
An unfortunate arrangement is one that has gone wrong, so the letters it governs are not lying in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, sixteen letters

annotation.surface: Advice to go to Italy, and a grumble that there is no time to hunt down pasta in Leeds.
annotation.walkthrough: The saying is an old traveller's boast about the bay: see it once and nothing afterwards can matter. 'The home of pizza' is the city itself rather than the country.
annotation.definitionFit: The proverb tells you to see the bay before you die, and the definition gives the same instruction the other way round, as a last request.

clue.text: Errant spud festering in lunchbox, say? (10)

definitions.note: 'Lunchbox' is a singular slang word for what the answer names in the plural, and it defines by example: one nickname for the region rather than a synonym.

indicators.note: Something festering is rotting where it lies, and letters left to rot do not keep the order they were given in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: A stray potato going bad at the bottom of somebody's packed lunch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lunchbox' is British tabloid slang for a man's genitals, coined at the sprinter Linford Christie's expense in the 1990s and never quite retired since.
annotation.definitionFit: lunchbox, say? → UNDERPARTS: the decorous term for the body's lower regions, of which the slang word is one cheerfully rude example.

clue.text: Small jumper back on top of littl’un, purchase jackets (7)

indicators.note: In a down entry these words say one piece sits above another, and the very same words hand over the top letter of the word behind them.
To jacket a thing is to put a coat round it, so this word closes over what sits between its two halves.

blocks.note: to and fro: fro is the old word for back, and it survives nowhere else
to purchase something is to get it
the first letter of that word is all 'top of' asks for

annotation.surface: A small pullover worn back to front over a little one, with coats bought to go over the top.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is a woolly garment all through the surface and a thing that jumps in the definition, and that is the whole distance between the clothes shop and the pond.
annotation.definitionFit: Small jumper → FROGLET: the -let ending makes it a young frog, and a frog is the standard example of a creature that gets about by jumping.

clue.text: Resentment in chap on bottling up grievances, initially (7)

indicators.note: Bottling something up keeps it shut inside, which is where the letter goes — in among what has already been put together.
'Initially' asks for the state a word is in at the start, which on the page comes down to its opening letter.

blocks.note: a dude is a chap
the little word is taken at face value and tacked straight on the end
the letter this word begins with, nothing looked up

annotation.surface: A man who swallows his complaints from the very beginning.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In high dudgeon' is the only phrase this noun survives in, so the definition is a word most solvers have met a hundred times without ever meeting it alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Resentment → DUDGEON: the offended, indignant sort of resentment, a noun that now travels almost solely in the phrase 'in high dudgeon'.

clue.text: Take back control, say (9)

blocks.note: to rein something is to control it, from the strap that steers a horse
to state something is to say it

annotation.surface: A political slogan about taking back control.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Take back control' was a referendum slogan, which is what makes the three words read as one phrase; the definition stops after two of them and the rest is wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Take back → REINSTATE: taking back a sacked employee or a scrapped rule is putting it in place again, the verb for restoring someone to a post.

clue.text: Robot managed corners by contrast in reverse (5)

indicators.note: To corner someone is to trap them with no way past, so this word closes round what it has caught.
'In reverse' means read the other way about, and this is an across entry, so those letters arrive right to left.

blocks.note: managed to do it comes to the same thing as did it
the word that offers the alternative, the one you reach for when setting one thing against another

annotation.surface: A machine that took the bends better going backwards.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In reverse' looks as though it belongs to the driving, and it is an instruction; what gets turned round is a two-letter word, which is why so little seems to happen.
annotation.definitionFit: Robot → DROID: the Star Wars clipping of android, now the general word for a humanoid robot in and out of the films.

clue.text: Force of a male sovereign a youth repelled to some extent (4)

indicators.note: Something repelled has been driven back the way it came, so the letters run right to left along this across entry.
'To some extent' says you want only part of what is in front of you, and the part wanted is a run of letters inside the words themselves.

blocks.note: four letters in a row straddle the two gaps between these words

annotation.surface: A young man fending off the power of a king.
annotation.walkthrough: Yin's opposite is the male, bright and active principle of Chinese thought, which is what the definition is describing rather than any king's authority.
annotation.definitionFit: Force of a male → YANG: in Chinese philosophy this is the masculine, active principle, set against the feminine yin.

clue.text: Primate in Renault kicking out first of churchgoers, one of those going on foot (10)

definitions.text: one of those going on foot

indicators.note: 'In' is the placement instruction: the primate is not beside the car but inside it, and so are its letters.
Kicking something out throws it off the premises, and the letter named next is thrown out of the word it was sitting in.
'First of' takes the single letter a word opens with and leaves the whole of the rest of it behind.

blocks.note: the Espace is Renault's people carrier, a name the marque has used for forty years
the C that word opens with is the letter kicked out, leaving five behind
the drill is a short-tailed West African monkey, a close relative of the mandrill

annotation.surface: A monkey riding in a car and shoving the first of the congregation out of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Primate' points hard at an archbishop in a clue already full of churchgoers, and the wordplay wants the monkey instead.
annotation.definitionFit: one of those going on foot → ESPADRILLE: the canvas shoe with a plaited rope sole, so what goes on foot is a shoe rather than a walker.

clue.text: Said craft at sea, lost ultimately – like that? (4,6)

definitions.text: Said craft at sea, lost ultimately – like that?

indicators.note: Being at sea is being all over the place with no bearings, which is exactly the state the letters in front of it have been left in.
'Ultimately' means in the end, so what is wanted from the word before it is the letter standing at its end.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
the last letter of losT joins the nine

annotation.surface: A boat reported missing somewhere out on the water.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word does both jobs: the sentence describes a vessel that has drifted away and the same words hand over the letters, which is what 'like that?' points back at.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight — a craft at sea and finally lost is in exactly this condition — so the sentence defines the state it also spells.

clue.text: Maiden visited by a dragon (6)

indicators.note: A visitor comes inside the house rather than standing at the gate, so what visits goes in among the letters instead of beside them.

blocks.note: the Maiden is the zodiac sign, the constellation drawn as a young woman
the article itself, dropped in whole

annotation.surface: A young woman receiving a visit from a dragon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dragon' is the definition and it is not the beast: a dragon is a fierce and domineering woman, which is what lets the fairy-tale surface run so smoothly.
annotation.definitionFit: dragon → VIRAGO: both name a fierce, overbearing woman, the answer being the formal literary word where 'dragon' is the everyday insult.

clue.text: Modest weight needed for support (5,2)

definitions.note: 'Support' is given in the plain form while the answer is past tense; the enumeration is what tells you to supply the tense yourself.

blocks.note: lean means spare or meagre, as in lean times — a modest amount of something
a ton is a unit of weight

annotation.surface: A small weight is all it takes to prop the thing up.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the whole difficulty: two ordinary words go in and the answer splits the same letters one place further along, into two quite different ones.
annotation.definitionFit: support → LEANT ON: to lean on a thing is to rest your weight against it and let it hold you up, which is taking support from it.

clue.text: Clue for dog (7)

blocks.note: a hint that points you towards the thing you are hunting for
the gun dog that stands rigid with its nose aimed at hidden game

annotation.surface: A hint towards which breed is meant.
annotation.walkthrough: Three clues in this grid read 'clue for dog' with a different word in front, and each answer is a breed that doubles as somebody's part in the crossword.
annotation.definitionFit: A pointer is a hint that points you towards the answer, and a pointer is the gun dog that freezes with its nose aimed at the game.

clue.text: Print error not quite covered up by press (7)

indicators.note: 'Not quite' the whole word stops just short of the end of it, so the final letter never arrives.
Being covered up by something means having it lie right over you, so the outer word closes round these letters.

blocks.note: to press a thing is to push it
a blip is a small error, and it turns up here a letter short

annotation.surface: A printing mistake hushed up by the newspapers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Press' is the newspaper trade all through the surface and the plain verb to push in the wordplay, which is what makes one sentence out of two halves.
annotation.definitionFit: Print → PUBLISH: both are verbs for putting words out into the world, though a publisher issues the book while a printer only manufactures it.

clue.text: Female film? (4,3)

blocks.note: the first two letters of that word are Fe, the chemical symbol for iron, taken from Latin ferrum
what is left of the word once those two letters go is male, and a male is a man

annotation.surface: A film with a woman at the heart of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay is one word long. Split 'Female' after two letters and a chemical symbol stands next to an ordinary noun, which is why the enumeration (4,3) looks impossible at first.
annotation.definitionFit: film? → IRON MAN: the 2008 Marvel film, so the definition names the class and the question mark admits this is one film among thousands.

clue.text: Writer of clue for dog (6)

blocks.note: the trade name for whoever composes a crossword, used by the papers themselves
the long-haired gun dog that drops to a crouch when it scents birds

annotation.surface: Whoever wrote a clue about a dog.
annotation.walkthrough: Paul is naming himself here: the word for whoever composes a crossword is also the long-haired gun dog, Irish or English or Gordon, that stands stock still on a scent.
annotation.definitionFit: The setter is the person who writes the clues in a crossword, and a setter is also a breed of gun dog trained to freeze when it finds birds.

clue.text: Cast a spell on an item of ‘ardware, we ‘ear? (7)

indicators.note: Hearing is the whole point, and the dropped aitch tells you which accent to hear it in before you write anything down.

blocks.note: the article stays exactly as the clue prints it
hardware runs to hammers, and the setter's apostrophe has already knocked the aitch off this one
said as one, the article and the tool run together into seven quite different letters

annotation.surface: A spell being cast over a piece of hardware, by all accounts.
annotation.walkthrough: The dropped aitches are printed rather than left to you: 'ardware is the setter putting the accent on the page, and the sound is the only route from tools to romance.
annotation.definitionFit: Cast a spell on → ENAMOUR: to enamour someone is to make them fall in love, which is charming them in the older, magical sense of that verb.

clue.text: Solver of clue for dog (10)

blocks.note: the dogged tracker of a person, who follows a trail until it gives out
the breed with the drooping ears and the celebrated nose, used to follow a scent

annotation.surface: Whoever finally works a clue about a dog out.
annotation.walkthrough: Third of the trio — clue, writer of clue, solver of clue — and the longest breed of the three, the one police forces use to follow a scent across country.
annotation.definitionFit: A bloodhound is the tracking dog with the celebrated nose, and the word is used of any dogged investigator who follows a trail to the end.

clue.text: Poodle, smut by one’s ears? (4)

indicators.note: Taking a word by the ears is judging it by the noise it makes, so what gets written down matches the sound and not the spelling.

blocks.note: smut is porn, and in an English accent that drops its r that word is exactly the noise wanted here

annotation.surface: A poodle with something filthy right by its ears.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poodle' is the dog theme's decoy: it means somebody's lapdog in the political sense, which is what got Tony Blair called George Bush's poodle.
annotation.definitionFit: Poodle → PAWN: a poodle is somebody's obedient creature and a pawn is the piece a stronger player pushes about, so both are another's instrument.

clue.text: Vile family missing daddy on vacation at first (5)

indicators.note: What is missing has been taken away, so the letters named next are the ones the longer word has to do without.
A word on vacation has been emptied out: everyone has left the middle and only the letters at the two ends are still standing there.
'At first' says where the loss falls — at the front of the word rather than anywhere else along it.

blocks.note: a dynasty is a ruling family, one generation handing on to the next
empty that word out and its first and last letters are left holding the ends

annotation.surface: A vile family away on holiday with the father not there.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' is a hard-working crossword idiom — it empties a word rather than sending it away — and what it empties out here is what then has to go missing.
annotation.definitionFit: Vile → NASTY: both are plain adjectives for something disgusting or spiteful, the answer being the everyday word where 'vile' is the stronger one.

clue.text: Beefcake learning to wipe bottom (4)

indicators.note: To wipe something is to rub it out altogether, so the letter pointed at is deleted rather than shifted elsewhere.
This is a down entry, so the bottom of the word is the letter standing at the foot of the column.

blocks.note: learning is study, the noun for what a student puts in

annotation.surface: A hunk learning to clean up after himself.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beefcake' is 1950s magazine slang for photographs of muscular men, the male answer to cheesecake, and it long ago came to mean the man himself.
annotation.definitionFit: Beefcake → STUD: both are slang for a conspicuously muscular and attractive man, the answer borrowed from the horse kept for breeding.

clue.text: What giant might say, though shorter – a few feet? (5)

indicators.note: Being shorter than what the giant actually said means the boast arrives with its final letter clipped off.

blocks.note: the plainest boast a giant could make about himself, run together as six letters

annotation.surface: A giant announcing his size, only not at full length.
annotation.walkthrough: Feet are the units a line of verse is measured in, and the answer is the Latin plural of the commonest one — the te-TUM beat of 'again' or 'delay'.
annotation.definitionFit: a few feet? → IAMBI: an iamb is a metrical foot in poetry, so a few of them are feet in the prosodic sense rather than the bodily one.

clue.text: Rabble-rousing idiots use bombs (9)

indicators.note: A show that bombs falls apart in front of the audience, and letters that fall apart do not land in the order they started in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: Fools with explosives, stirring up trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bombs' sits at the end of the clue where a solver expects the definition, and it is the instruction; the definition is the very first word instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Rabble-rousing → SEDITIOUS: both are adjectives for speech that stirs people up against the authorities, the answer being the word the law uses.

clue.text: On passing through, come across Devon town (7)

indicators.note: Whatever passes through a place goes in one side and out the other, so this piece ends up inside the letters rather than alongside them.

blocks.note: to hit on an idea is to come across it
the clue's first word goes in as it stands, both its letters

annotation.surface: Stopping off in a Devon town while travelling through.
annotation.walkthrough: Honiton is the small market town in east Devon on the old road to Exeter, known for two centuries for its handmade lace.
annotation.definitionFit: Devon town → HONITON: a real market town in east Devon, so the definition names the class and the answer supplies one instance of it.

clue.text: Wrinkled – in the manner of a tree? (7)

blocks.note: the elder is the hedgerow tree that gives us elderflower and elderberry
-ly is the ending English tacks on to mean in the manner of, as in slowly or kindly

annotation.surface: Something creased like the bark of a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads back to front: the ending is named first and the tree second, so the assembly runs the opposite way to the sentence you are given.
annotation.definitionFit: Wrinkled → ELDERLY: not a synonym but the sign of the thing, since lined skin is what the polite adjective for old is pointing at here.
